stories.headline: Two U.S. Navy Fighter Jets Collide Mid-Air at Idaho Air Show; All Four Crew Eject Safely
stories.summary:
Two U.S. Navy EA-18G Growler jets collided in mid-air Sunday during an aerial demonstration at the Gunfighter Skies air show in Idaho. All four crew members aboard the two aircraft successfully ejected and are reported to be in stable condition.

The dramatic incident occurred on the second and final day of the event. Video of the collision circulated widely, showing the moment of impact during what was intended to be a routine performance maneuver. The Navy has not yet announced the cause of the collision or whether an investigation is underway.

The EA-18G Growler is an electronic warfare variant of the F/A-18F Super Hornet and serves as a frontline aircraft in the U.S. Navy's fleet. Mid-air collisions at air shows, while rare, have historically resulted in significant casualties; the safe ejection of all four crew members in this instance is being treated as a fortunate outcome. The story is being covered by eight major outlets.

stories.headline: Iran Executions of Political Prisoners Surge Since U.S.-Israeli Strike, UN Warns
stories.summary:
Since the United States and Israel struck Iran on February 28, the United Nations has verified the execution of at least 32 political prisoners in the country, according to a BBC investigation. The surge represents a sharp increase over 2025, when Amnesty International recorded 45 politically motivated executions across the entire year. UN human rights officials say the death penalty is increasingly being deployed to suppress dissent.

Among those executed was Mehrab Abdollahzadeh, arrested in 2022 during protests following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini and accused of involvement in the killing of a Basij militia member. He recorded a voice note from death row asserting his innocence and alleging forced confessions extracted through torture. Fourteen of those executed this year were arrested in connection with a January uprising that was itself suppressed with lethal force, resulting in thousands of deaths.

Human rights groups say Iran carried out 2,159 executions in 2025 — the highest since 1989 — with the vast majority for drug offenses or murder. Analysts at the Kurdistan Human Rights Network say the regime is using intensified repression to project authority after its image was damaged by domestic unrest and the ongoing war. The UN has expressed concern that some executions are occurring in secret.

stories.headline: LIRR Strike Halts Service for 300,000 Daily Riders, Costing Region $61 Million a Day
stories.summary:
Five unions representing approximately 3,500 Long Island Rail Road workers went on strike Saturday, shutting down service for roughly 300,000 daily commuters between Long Island and New York City. New York State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli estimated the economic toll at $61 million per day, with widespread road congestion adding to the regional disruption.

The unions involved — representing engineers, signalmen and machinists — rejected the MTA's final offer, which included the equivalent of a 4.5% pay raise for a fourth contract year. Other MTA unions had previously accepted a 9.5% raise covering the prior three years. The unions' demands, which the MTA said would translate into an 8% fare hike, come as average cash compensation for members of the striking unions already exceeds $136,000 annually, according to MTA figures.

The blame has been distributed in multiple directions. Governor Kathy Hochul attributed the strike to the Trump administration cutting off federal mediation prematurely; Trump and GOP gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman criticized Hochul for failing to prevent the walkout. Union leaders countered that management's offers were inadequate. Workers' contracts expired three years ago. The strike highlights ongoing tension between public-sector labor agreements and fiscal constraints on transit systems serving major metropolitan areas.

stories.headline: Thousands Gather on National Mall for Christian Prayer Rally Tied to U.S. 250th Anniversary
stories.summary:
Thousands of people descended on Washington's National Mall on Sunday for "Rededicate 250: National Jubilee of Prayer, Praise & Thanksgiving," a daylong Christian prayer rally billed as a rededication of the United States as "One Nation under God" in honor of the country's 250th anniversary. President Trump delivered a video address to the gathering, while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and House Speaker Mike Johnson appeared in person or via promotional materials.

The event's lineup was almost exclusively Christian, with the sole non-Christian speaker being Orthodox Jewish Rabbi Meir Soloveichik, who serves on the Trump administration's Religious Liberty Commission. The stage featured imagery associating the nation's founders with Christian symbolism, including a white cross displayed within arched stained-glass windows designed to resemble a federal building.

Critics from religious and civil society organizations pushed back sharply. The Rev. Adam Russell Taylor of the progressive Christian group Sojourners said the event represented a "rededication" to "a very narrow and ideological part of the Christian faith that betrays our nation's fundamental commitment to religious freedom." Rabbi Jonah Dov Pesner of the Religious Action Center of Reform Judaism emphasized America's historic religious diversity, including Jews, Muslims, and Indigenous peoples from the nation's earliest days.

Supporters framed the rally as a return to what they described as the country's founding principles, with Hegseth stating in a promotional video that rights come from God, not government, and that national strength is rooted in faith. The event highlights ongoing tensions over the role of Christianity in American public life as the country marks its semiseptennial.

stories.headline: Oldest Known Manuscript of First English Poem Discovered in Roman Library
stories.summary:
Researchers at Trinity College Dublin have identified what they believe to be the oldest surviving manuscript copy of "Caedmon's Hymn," widely considered the first poem written in the English language, in Rome's main public library. The manuscript dates to the 9th century — roughly three centuries older than the previously known earliest copy — and is significant because the Old English poem appears within the main body of the Latin text rather than as a marginal addition or appendix.

"Caedmon's Hymn" is a nine-line poem composed in Old English by a Northumbrian agricultural worker in the 7th century, according to an account preserved by the monk and historian the Venerable Bede. The poem is said to have been produced after a divine vision instructed Caedmon, who worked at Whitby Abbey in North Yorkshire, to sing about creation. Associate professor Mark Faulkner of Trinity College Dublin described the discovery as evidence that English was already being treated as a language of cultural importance by the early 9th century, long before scholars previously assumed.

The manuscript had crossed the Atlantic at least twice and changed hands multiple times before researchers located it digitally in Rome. Visiting research fellow Elisabetta Magnanti, who co-led the discovery, said the team was "speechless" upon finding the poem integrated into the main Latin text rather than relegated to the margins.

Faulkner described the find as pushing back the documented diffusion of the English language by roughly three centuries, offering new insight into how early medieval scholars valued vernacular writing alongside Latin scholarship.

stories.headline: Comey Fires Back at Acting AG Blanche Over Federal Case, Cites Court Rules on Public Comment
stories.summary:
Former FBI Director James Comey publicly challenged Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday, urging him to "bone up on the rules" after Blanche made public statements about the ongoing federal case against Comey. Comey, who faces prosecution related to a 2025 Instagram post, declined to discuss the substance of the case, citing federal court rules that restrict parties from making extrajudicial statements about pending litigation.

Comey stated he has "complete faith in our judicial system" and appeared to draw a pointed contrast between his own restraint and what he characterized as Blanche's improper public commentary on an active case. The remark carries additional weight given that Blanche previously served as Donald Trump's personal criminal defense attorney before being appointed to lead the Justice Department.

The case against Comey is part of a broader pattern of the Trump Justice Department pursuing legal action against individuals perceived as adversaries of the president, a practice that critics — primarily Democrats and civil liberties advocates — have called the weaponization of federal law enforcement. Supporters of the prosecutions argue they represent the legitimate application of the law to officials who themselves overstepped their authority.

Separately, the story broke on the same day as continued disruption to the Long Island Rail Road, where workers remain on strike for the first time in roughly three decades, affecting hundreds of thousands of daily commuters in the New York metropolitan area.

stories.headline: Trump Warns Iran 'Clock Is Ticking,' Raises Prospect of Harder Military Strikes
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump issued a stark public warning to Iran on Sunday, writing on Truth Social that 'the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST, or there won't be anything left of them.' The warning came as U.S.-Iran nuclear negotiations appeared stalled, with Iranian officials refusing to make meaningful concessions on their nuclear program and rejecting several American demands.

According to Axios, which spoke with Trump directly, the president indicated that if Tehran does not produce a better offer, military options are back on the table. U.S. officials say Trump wants a negotiated deal but that Iran's posture has frustrated progress. Trump is reportedly expected to convene senior national security advisers to weigh next steps.

The warning follows Trump's return from Beijing, where trade discussions with China dominated his agenda, and comes amid reports that he had previously signaled openness to a 20-year suspension arrangement on Iran's nuclear activities — a position that appeared to harden with Sunday's statement. Iran has not publicly responded to the latest threat.

Supporters of Trump's approach argue that maximum-pressure rhetoric is necessary to force concessions from Tehran, while critics warn that inflammatory language risks miscalculation and military conflict in an already volatile Middle East. The standoff has implications for global oil markets and U.S. alliances in the region.

stories.headline: Ronda Rousey Submits Gina Carano in 17 Seconds in MMA Comeback Bout
stories.summary:
Ronda Rousey returned to mixed martial arts after a 9.5-year absence on Saturday night, submitting Gina Carano with her signature armbar just 17 seconds into their joint comeback bout. The 39-year-old Rousey immediately charged Carano after the opening bell, secured a takedown, and applied the finish with characteristic speed, reaffirming her status as one of the sport's all-time figures before announcing her retirement.

Carano, 44, had not competed in 17 years before Saturday's fight and was visibly good-natured about the swift outcome, hugging Rousey after the stoppage. 'I wanted that to last longer,' Carano said. 'I felt so ready. I've never felt that good. But I haven't been here for 17 years.' Rousey described the finish as 'beautiful martial arts' and said she was motivated in part by having her husband and children watching.

Rousey became one of the most famous athletes in the world during her UFC run in the 2010s, winning the first women's title in the organization's history and helping legitimize women's MMA as a mainstream sport. Her return was driven, she said, by a desire to reconnect with her love of martial arts after stepping away following back-to-back losses. She has stated this bout is the final chapter of her competitive career.

The fight drew significant attention given both fighters' cultural prominence beyond sports — Rousey as a trailblazer in women's combat sports and Hollywood, and Carano as a film and television actress whose career has carried its own political dimension in recent years.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Launches Massive Drone Strike on Moscow Region, Killing Three
stories.summary:
Ukraine carried out its largest drone attack on the Moscow region in more than a year overnight, with Russian officials reporting at least three people killed and several injured. A woman died in the city of Khimki north of Moscow, while a man and a woman were killed in the village of Pogorelki. Russia's military said it intercepted 556 drones across the country, approximately 130 of them in the Moscow region. An Indian citizen was also killed, according to India's Moscow embassy.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called the strikes an 'entirely justified' response to recent deadly Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, including a massive missile and drone barrage earlier this week that killed 24 people in Kyiv. Ukraine's state security service said it targeted oil facilities, a semiconductor-making plant, and air defense systems at the Belbek military airfield in Crimea. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported 12 people injured after drones struck an entrance to the city's oil refinery, with three nearby houses also damaged.

Russia's busiest airport, Sheremetyevo, reported drone wreckage on its territory but said no one was injured and operations remained stable. The scale of the attack represents a significant escalation in Ukraine's long-range strike campaign against Russian infrastructure and signals Kyiv's intent to bring the costs of war directly to Russian territory. Zelensky stated that Ukraine's 'long-range sanctions have reached the Moscow region' and warned that 'their state must end its war.'

The exchange of strikes underscores the continued intensity of the conflict even as diplomatic discussions around a potential ceasefire remain inconclusive. The attack marks a concrete new development in the Russia-Ukraine war, with the largest drone assault on the Russian capital region in over a year occurring overnight into Sunday.

stories.headline: Venezuela Deports Maduro Ally Alex Saab to United States for Criminal Proceedings
stories.summary:
Venezuela's government announced Saturday that it had deported Alex Saab, a close ally of former President Nicolás Maduro and a Colombian-born businessman long described by U.S. officials as Maduro's 'bag man,' to the United States to face multiple criminal investigations. The move marks a dramatic reversal: Maduro's government previously fought strenuously to protect Saab after his international arrest in 2020, and Saab was returned to Venezuela in 2023 as part of a prisoner swap brokered under the Biden administration. Venezuelan authorities referred to Saab only as a 'Colombian citizen' in their statement, an apparent workaround of Venezuelan law prohibiting the extradition of its own nationals.

Saab, 54, amassed significant wealth through Venezuelan government contracts and is now expected to potentially testify against Maduro, who is himself awaiting trial on drug trafficking charges in Manhattan after being captured in a U.S. military raid in January. Federal prosecutors have been investigating Saab's alleged role in a bribery conspiracy involving Venezuelan government contracts to import food. His removal to the U.S. is seen as part of the broader accommodation the new Venezuelan leadership under acting President Delcy Rodríguez has made toward Washington, including opening the country's oil and mining industries to American investment.

The deportation is likely to deepen internal divisions within Venezuela's ruling Chavista coalition. Hardliners such as Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, who himself faces U.S. criminal charges and wields significant influence over Venezuelan security forces, have bristled at Rodríguez's concessions to what the movement historically has called the U.S. 'Empire.' Saab had already been demoted and effectively sidelined by the new leadership before his removal.

The case carries significant geopolitical weight, coming months after the U.S. military's capture of Maduro himself and amid ongoing U.S. efforts to reshape its relationship with Venezuela. Saab's potential cooperation with U.S. prosecutors could provide prosecutors with a high-value inside witness against Maduro and other senior Venezuelan officials.

stories.headline: Update: Modena Car-Ramming Attack Suspect Had Prior Mental Health Referral; Italian Leaders Visit Victims
stories.summary:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and President Sergio Mattarella visited victims in hospital on Sunday following Saturday's car-ramming and stabbing attack in Modena, in which a man drove into a crowd of pedestrians injuring eight people, four seriously. One woman had both legs amputated. The suspect, a 31-year-old Italian national of Moroccan origin identified by far-right Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini as Salim El Koudri, had been referred to a mental health center in 2022 for schizoid disorders but had 'disappeared without a trace' afterward, the city prefect said.

Meloni, who canceled a planned trip to Cyprus to respond to the incident, called it 'extremely serious' and praised a bystander, Luca Signorelli, who chased the attacker after the vehicle came to a halt, was attacked with a knife, and then helped restrain the suspect with other passersby. Italian media describe the suspect as an economics graduate who is unemployed and has no prior criminal record. The attack occurred in the afternoon near Modena's iconic cathedral on a busy pedestrian street.

The incident has immediately become politically charged in Italy. Salvini, who leads the anti-immigrant League party, posted the suspect's name on social media, framing the attack in the context of immigration. Critics noted that the suspect was born in Italy and had no criminal record, and that authorities identified mental illness as a likely factor. The tension between those emphasizing the attacker's ethnic background and those highlighting his mental health history reflects ongoing national debates about immigration, integration, and public safety.

This story represents a new development on a previously covered event: Italian leaders' hospital visits, the revelation of the suspect's prior mental health referral, and Meloni's public response all occurred Sunday and materially advance the story beyond Saturday's initial report.

stories.headline: Peru Officially Confirms Fujimori and Sánchez as Presidential Runoff Candidates for June 7 Vote
stories.summary:
Peruvian electoral authorities have officially certified conservative Keiko Fujimori and left-wing lawmaker Roberto Sánchez as the two candidates who will compete in a presidential runoff election on June 7, more than a month after the first round of voting was held. The formal confirmation sets the stage for a sharp ideological contest in one of South America's larger economies.

Fujimori, daughter of jailed former President Alberto Fujimori, is a veteran of Peruvian presidential politics, having lost runoff elections in 2011 and 2016. She leads the Fuerza Popular party and represents a right-of-center platform. Sánchez, a sitting lawmaker, enters the runoff as the left-wing challenger in a country that has seen significant political instability in recent years, including the impeachment and imprisonment of former President Pedro Castillo.

Peru's political landscape has been highly volatile, with multiple presidents removed from office or forced to resign over the past decade. The June 7 runoff will determine the country's direction on economic policy, relations with mining and energy industries that are central to Peru's export economy, and ongoing anti-corruption efforts. International observers and markets will be watching the result closely given Peru's role as one of the world's leading copper producers.

stories.headline: UAE's Barakah Nuclear Power Plant Struck by Drone, Fire Breaks Out
stories.summary:
A fire broke out at the United Arab Emirates' Barakah Nuclear Power Plant on Sunday after a drone strike hit the area, according to reports. Abu Dhabi's state media office did not attribute the strike to any party and urged the public to rely only on verified sources and to avoid spreading rumors about the incident.

The Barakah plant, located in Abu Dhabi emirate, is the Arab world's first operational nuclear power station and a critical piece of the UAE's energy infrastructure. A strike on the facility would represent a significant escalation in the regional conflict stemming from the U.S.-Israel military campaign against Iran, which has already seen Iranian attacks paralyze Qatar's gas exports and disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Details remain limited as authorities have not confirmed the source of the drone or the extent of damage to the facility. The incident underscores the expanding geographic footprint of the Iran conflict, with Gulf state infrastructure now apparently within range of hostile drone operations.

The UAE has maintained a delicate posture during the Iran conflict, and an attack on its nuclear facility — if confirmed as hostile — could significantly alter the regional calculus and draw additional Gulf states more directly into the confrontation.

stories.headline: Thousands March in Montgomery to Defend Black Voting Rights as Redistricting Rollbacks Accelerate
stories.summary:
Thousands of demonstrators rallied Saturday in Montgomery, Alabama — retracing the route of the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery Voting Rights March — to protest the dismantling of congressional districts that have provided Black political representation. The rally began in Selma and ended at the Alabama State Capitol, where Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) called Montgomery 'sacred soil' and warned that the current generation risked losing hard-won civil rights gains.

Organizers and speakers pointed to a series of Supreme Court decisions that have progressively weakened the Voting Rights Act, culminating in a recent ruling involving Louisiana that critics say cleared the way for stricter voter ID laws, tighter registration rules, and limits on early voting in states with histories of racial discrimination in elections. Veterans of the original Civil Rights Movement expressed alarm at the speed of the rollbacks.

Supporters of the redistricting changes argue that race-neutral mapping criteria produce fairer maps and that the Supreme Court rulings correctly interpret the law. Conservative legal groups contend that majority-minority districts can themselves constitute racial gerrymandering and that the focus should be on individual voting rights rather than group representation.

The rally drew participants from across the country and reflected growing Democratic and civil rights coalition efforts to mobilize voters ahead of midterm elections, framing redistricting fights as a central front in a broader struggle over political representation.

stories.headline: PGA Championship Final Round Set: Unheralded Alex Smalley Enters Sunday as 54-Hole Leader
stories.summary:
Alex Smalley, a 29-year-old PGA Tour journeyman with no prior Tour victories, enters Sunday's final round of the PGA Championship at Aronimink Golf Club holding a two-shot lead — the most unlikely position of his professional career. Smalley, a Duke University alumnus who turned professional in 2019, has made 85 cuts and recorded 15 top-10 finishes in 140 Tour starts but has never won on Tour.

The storyline surrounding Smalley extends beyond the leaderboard. His mother Maria has tracked his detailed tournament statistics — distance to the pin, club selection, wind direction — since his senior year of high school, and has attended virtually every event of his professional career, including this week at Aronimink.

A Smalley victory Sunday would rank among the more surprising major championship wins in recent memory, coming against a field that includes world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler and numerous other top-ranked players. The PGA Championship is the second major of the 2026 golf calendar.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Leaves Beijing with Boeing Deal Claim but No Confirmed Trade Breakthroughs
stories.summary:
President Trump departed Beijing after a two-day summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, declaring the talks "very successful" and claiming China had agreed to purchase 200 Boeing jets with a potential commitment for an additional 750 planes — Boeing's first major Chinese deal in nearly a decade. Trump also said American farmers would benefit from Chinese purchases of "billions of dollars" in soybeans. Xi called the visit "historic and landmark" and confirmed he will visit the White House in September.

However, no formal trade agreements were announced by either side, and Chinese officials did not confirm the Boeing deal or agricultural purchases. Notably, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that he and Xi did not discuss tariffs at all — a surprise given that a tariff truce struck in October is set to expire in November. The White House said both leaders agreed to create a "Board of Trade" to manage the bilateral relationship without reopening tariff negotiations.

The summit was heavy on symbolism: Trump received an honor guard, a state banquet, and an invitation to the exclusive compound where China's Communist Party leaders reside. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he expected progress on a mechanism to support future investment, but provided few specifics. Markets fell last week on the lack of concrete outcomes.

The divergence between Trump's bullish public characterization and the absence of Chinese confirmation has raised questions about what, if anything, was actually agreed. Analysts note that even the Boeing figure — if real — would represent a significant de-escalation in bilateral trade tensions that had effectively frozen American aerospace exports to China for years.

stories.headline: Two Convictions for Chinese Espionage in U.S. Coincide with Trump-Xi Summit
stories.summary:
A New York jury found Lu Jianwang, 64, president of a Chinese community association in Manhattan, guilty this week of acting as an unauthorized foreign agent for China after the FBI raided his Chinatown office in 2022 and accused him of operating the first known Chinese overseas police station on U.S. soil. Lu faces up to 30 years in prison. In a separate case, Arcadia, California Mayor Eileen Wang pleaded guilty to posting Chinese government propaganda targeting Chinese American communities on a website at Beijing's direction.

The two convictions came in the same week that President Trump traveled to Beijing for his summit with Xi Jinping — a meeting in which espionage was notably absent from the agenda as both sides focused on trade. Experts say the cases illustrate a pattern of Chinese efforts to suppress dissent and shape narratives among overseas Chinese communities, with at least 100 similar alleged police stations reported across 53 countries.

China has denied the stations are police outposts, with its Ministry of Public Security describing them in 2023 as volunteer centers helping citizens with administrative tasks such as driver's license renewals. A London police investigation into similar facilities concluded no criminal activity had occurred there. The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not respond to requests for comment.

Security analysts say the cases reflect a broader and intensifying Chinese influence campaign that combines soft power — funding overseas projects and institutions — with covert operations. "It's part of the same strategic approach, which is to tamp down on dissent and to shape a clear narrative around the PRC, and to do that in bolder ways," said Lauryn Williams of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

stories.headline: Bulgaria Wins Eurovision 2026 as UK Finishes Last with Single Point
stories.summary:
Bulgaria claimed victory at Eurovision 2026, with Israel finishing second after a close public vote. The competition, held this year in Europe, drew widespread attention for Ukraine's entry, which set a record for the contest's longest-ever sustained note. The UK, represented by musician Sam Battle — known as Look Mum No Computer — finished last for the third time since 2020, receiving one point from juries and zero from the public vote with the synth-pop entry "Eins, Zwei, Drei."

The result renewed debate in Britain about the BBC's approach to the contest. Critics argued the corporation treated Eurovision as a novelty event rather than a serious musical competition, while the broadcaster's defenders noted it took a deliberate creative risk on an unconventional entry. The UK's sole top-10 finish in the past 15 years came in 2022 when Sam Ryder placed second with a polished glam-rock entry widely praised as a genuine competitive effort.

Eurovision draws television audiences of roughly 160 million across Europe and beyond, making the UK's repeated last-place finishes a recurring point of national cultural conversation. Commentators noted that political voting patterns, song quality, and staging all factor into results, and that the UK's track record suggests systemic issues rather than a single bad year.

stories.headline: FIFA Faces Backlash Over Soaring World Cup Ticket Prices Ahead of U.S. Tournament
stories.summary:
FIFA is drawing sharp criticism for ticket prices at the 2026 World Cup, which will be hosted across the United States, Canada, and Mexico beginning in June. The average resale price for the cheapest group-stage tickets stood at $553 as of last week, according to analytics firm TicketData, while the least expensive available ticket for the July 19 final at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey was listed at $7,734. FIFA last week tripled prices for top seats at the final to $33,970, and secondary markets have shown some tickets listed above $45,000.

President Trump said he personally would not pay $1,000 to attend the U.S. opener, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta sent a letter to FIFA seeking answers about potentially misleading ticketing practices — specifically reports that FIFA sold tickets based on seat categories shown on stadium maps and later altered those categorizations before assigning precise seat locations. FIFA President Gianni Infantino defended the pricing, saying that extreme resale prices do not reflect face value and do not necessarily mean anyone will pay them.

Beyond tickets, host cities face significant ancillary costs. New Jersey Transit announced round-trip train fares from Manhattan to MetLife Stadium will be $98 per World Cup game, compared to the usual $13, citing an estimated $48 million cost to run tournament rail service. FIFA's requirement that host cities fund security and transportation has drawn additional scrutiny, though federal FEMA funding is expected to offset some expenses.

The 2026 tournament is the largest in World Cup history, expanded from 32 to 48 teams with 104 matches, and is projected to generate a record $10.9 billion in revenue. Critics argue FIFA's fee structure — collecting 15 percent from both buyer and seller on its official resale marketplace — compounds accessibility concerns for ordinary fans.
